title: A Deadly Password at the River
overview: After Jephthah's victory, a quarrel over pride and insults turns into a bloody war between Israelite tribes, followed by brief notes on three later leaders.

parts.label: Ephraim's angry complaint (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Ephraim, a large and powerful tribe west of the Jordan River, was offended at being left out of the victory and threatened to burn Jephthah alive in his house, much as it had complained to Gideon earlier (chapter 8). Jephthah answers that he did call them and they never came, so he risked his life and the LORD gave him the win.

parts.label: An insult turns into war (v. 4)
parts.note: The Ephraimites mocked the people of Gilead, Israelites living east of the Jordan, as runaways who did not truly belong, and Jephthah's men answered by fighting them. The exact wording of the insult is unclear in the original Hebrew, but its scorn is plain.

parts.label: The Shibboleth test (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Gilead's men held the river crossings and made anyone crossing say "Shibboleth" (a word that can mean a stream or an ear of grain); people from Ephraim said "s" for "sh," so their accent gave them away and they were killed. This is Israelites slaughtering Israelites, and some scholars think the word for "thousand" can mean a military unit, so the size of the number is debated.

parts.label: Jephthah's death (v. 7)
parts.note: Jephthah led Israel for six years and was buried in his home region of Gilead. The New Testament later lists him among people of faith (Hebrews 11), though many readers find his story deeply troubling.

parts.label: Three lesser-known leaders (vv. 8-15)
parts.note: Ibzan, Elon and Abdon get only brief notes on family, years of leadership and burial place, and Ibzan's Bethlehem may be a town in Zebulun rather than the famous one. Many readers take the big families, marriages outside the clan and seventy donkeys as signs of wealth and standing, though the text itself does not explain them.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jephthah should be read mainly as a hero of faith, as the New Testament lists him, or mainly as a warning sign of how violent and divided Israel had become in this period.
think: When have you seen a small difference, like an accent, a word or a label, used to decide who belongs, and what gives such small things so much power?
